- Mitochondrial & Cellular Energy Starvation (Glutamine, Butyrate, TCA Intermediates): Your gut barrier requires massive amounts of immediate, localized energy to maintain tight junction integrity. If your enterocytes (small intestine) or colonocytes (large intestine) lack their preferred mitochondrial fuels, the barrier structurally collapses, allowing lipopolysaccharides (LPS) and endotoxins to leak into systemic circulation.

    - L-Glutamine ([watch Dr. Rhonda vid](https://m.youtube.com/watch?v=5DVUEKrekYw&ra=m)): The absolute premier energy substrate for enterocytes and activated immune cells. It bypasses complex digestive steps, converting directly into alpha-ketoglutarate (α-KG) inside the mitochondria to power the citric acid cycle. This immediate cellular energy hit actively drives the repair of the gut mucosal barrier and prevents LPS translocation.

      - Dosing: Use 5g daily as a baseline to counter the gut mucosal breakdown caused by high-intensity or high-volume training (like CrossFit or intense cardio). Titrate up to 10–30g daily during acute immune exposure, high systemic stress, or if you are dealing with active IBD (Crohn's/Colitis).

      - The Cancer Caveat: Because hyper-proliferative cancer cells can also hijack glutamine to fuel their rapid replication, avoid high-dose protocol titrations if you have an active, existing colon or liver malignancy (the liver sees it first via portal vein delivery).

    - Butyrate & SCFAs: While the small intestine runs on glutamine, the large intestine relies on short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) like butyrate. Getting these via raw resistant starch fermentation or your home-brewed SIBO yogurt fuels colonocytes, locks down the lower gut barrier, and systematically suppresses inflammatory signals.

    - TCA Cycle Intermediates (Malic & Citric Acid): Organic acids like malate and citrate feed directly into the exact same mitochondrial energy pathways as glutamine. Consuming clean, sour profiles—such as organic malic acid, tart cherries, or green apples—provides rapid, alternative fuel to gut epithelial cells, accelerating mucosal healing from a different biochemical angle.
rewrite:
- Mitochondrial and cellular energy starvation: your gut barrier needs a huge amount of energy to keep its tight junctions intact, and the cells need that energy immediately, in the gut itself. The cells lining your small intestine are called enterocytes; the ones in your large intestine are colonocytes. When their mitochondria don't get their preferred fuels, the barrier falls apart, letting lipopolysaccharides (LPS, from bacterial cell walls) and other endotoxins leak into your bloodstream.

    - L-Glutamine ([watch Dr. Rhonda vid](https://m.youtube.com/watch?v=5DVUEKrekYw&ra=m)): Glutamine gives your gut lining the immediate energy that drives its repair and stops LPS from getting through. It's by far the best fuel for those small intestine cells, and for your immune cells when they're activated. It skips the complicated digestive steps. Inside the mitochondria, it converts directly into alpha-ketoglutarate (α-KG), which powers the citric acid cycle, the process mitochondria use to make energy.

      - Take 5g a day as a baseline to counter the breakdown of the gut lining from high-intensity or high-volume training (like CrossFit or intense cardio). Raise it gradually to 10-30g a day during an acute immune exposure or when your whole system is under a lot of stress. For active IBD (Crohn's or colitis), use that same gradual increase.

      - CAUTION: Cancer cells that multiply very fast can also use glutamine to fuel that growth. Don't raise it to the high doses if you have active colon or liver cancer. The liver gets the glutamine first, through the portal vein.

    - The small intestine runs on glutamine, but your colon cells rely on butyrate and other short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) for fuel. These keep the lower gut barrier sealed, and they also keep suppressing inflammatory signals. You get them when your gut bacteria ferment raw resistant starch, or from your home-brewed SIBO yogurt.

    - Malic and citric acid (TCA cycle intermediates): Organic acids like malate and citrate go straight into the same mitochondrial energy pathways as glutamine. The cells lining your gut get a quick alternative fuel, and supplying those pathways with these acids speeds up healing of the lining through another biochemical route. Use clean, sour things such as organic malic acid. Tart cherries and green apples are food options too.

original: The best general commercial stack I have seen so far is Microbiome Labs Total Gut Restoration, because it combines probiotic, prebiotic, and mucosal-support components. For a more leaky-gut-specific stack, Dr. Ruscio's Leaky Gut Support Kit is a reasonable option. For a single gut-lining repair formula, Designs for Health GI Revive is one of the more complete products, but it should be understood as a repair product, not a complete gut protocol by itself.

That said, some people want a ready-made starting point rather than buying every ingredient separately. For a general "repair and rebuild" approach, I would look for a stack that covers three categories:

1. Microbiome support: a well-tolerated probiotic or probiotic system

2. Prebiotic / butyrate support: something that helps short-chain fatty acid production, especially butyrate

3. Barrier repair: nutrients that support the gut lining, such as glutamine, zinc carnosine, colostrum, mucosal-support herbs, or similar compounds
